title: Appendix B: Four Practical System Designs

sections.title: Choosing Between Push, Pull, and Both
The Product Contract and Its Authority
An API That Distinguishes Evaluation from Execution
What the Designs Have in Common

html:
A URL shortener, a social timeline, and a notification service can each be sketched with a small number of components. That sketch leaves important decisions unresolved: how much processing the first deployment must support, which records identify repeated operations, where data is stored, and what the service does when a dependency stops responding.

Each design starts with the behavior a customer needs. The traffic and failure assumptions then determine which components are necessary. The arithmetic is shown so that readers can replace the assumptions with figures from another workload. Each design also includes a failure drill that checks a different part of its contract.

Applying the Design Review

Chapter 14 established five questions for reviewing an architecture: what the application promises, what each request requires, what survives interruption, what happens at a resource limit, and which measurements would change the decision. We will use those questions in four different domains rather than repeat the framework here.

The URL shortener begins with one durable code-to-destination mapping. The social timeline introduces fan-out and freshness. Notifications add delayed delivery and provider recovery. The change-validation platform requires versioned policy authority and a deployment enforcement boundary. Each design begins with a plausible small implementation and adds components only when the requirements justify them.

A URL Shortener

What the Service Promises

Given a short code, the service sends the visitor to the destination the creator chose, within milliseconds, for as long as the link is active. Two consequences of that sentence matter more than they first appear. A link that has been disabled, because it was abusive or its owner deleted it, has to stop redirecting within a bounded time. And a code, once issued, must never point somewhere else.

Sizing the Service

Suppose the service creates 50 million links a month and receives about 100 redirects for every link created.

Seven base-62 characters provide about 3.5×10123.5\times10^{12}3.5×1012 codes, and five years of creations would use about 0.085 percent of that space. This leaves room to choose between allocation schemes, although random allocation still requires collision handling. The estimated creation rate is about 19 per second, compared with 1,930 redirects per second. Test the combined workload, including administrative updates, before choosing the database size.

Where Capacity Runs Out

The first capacity test should target peak cache misses. The store must serve redirects that miss the cache, including a cold-cache recovery interval. If the cache serves 90 percent of redirects, the database receives about 960 lookups per second at the 9,600 peak, which one primary or replica must demonstrate in a workload test. At a 50 percent hit rate it receives 4,800, and that higher rate needs its own capacity test. The hit rate is an assumption the whole design rests on, and it belongs in the hidden-assumptions review with a measurement and a threshold, as Chapter 5 treated it.

Generating Short Codes

Creation needs a code that no earlier creation has used, and there are four approaches to compare. Each fails differently, so Table Table lays them side by side before we choose.

The fourth approach works well here. Each creation instance leases a block of identifiers, say 10,000, from a central allocator and hands them out locally. With four creation instances, each contacts the allocator about once every half hour at this rate. Before a number becomes a code, it passes through a small permutation, so that sequential counters produce codes with no visible pattern. Listing Listing shows one way to do it.

The permutation uses a Feistel network. It splits a number into two halves and repeatedly mixes one half into the other. The construction is a permutation regardless of the mixing function, which ensures that distinct inputs produce distinct outputs. The catch is that its range is a power of two, here 2422^{42}242, and our code space is 62762^7627, which is smaller. The loop is what handles the mismatch. If the permutation produces a number outside the code space, we apply it again until the number falls within the permitted range. This is called cycle walking, and because 2422^{42}242 is only 1.25 times larger than 62762^7627, a near-uniform permutation needs about 1.25 passes on average. Roughly 20 percent of first results fall outside the code space. Running the code over the first million counters produced a million distinct seven-character codes.

The permutation obscures the relationship between sequential identifiers, which makes adjacent codes harder to recognize by inspection. It provides no cryptographic protection against systematic guessing or enumeration. If the service requires unpredictable codes, generate them using a cryptographically secure random generator and enforce uniqueness in the database, or adopt a vetted format-preserving cipher. This illustrative Feistel construction must not be used as a security control.

The uniqueness guarantee itself comes from the database, not from the allocator. The link table enforces a unique constraint on the code, so a bug in the allocator shows up as a rejected write instead of a visitor sent to the wrong page. Creation requests include an operation identifier supplied by the client, so a retry after a timeout returns the code already issued instead of minting a second one. That is the idea behind the payment operation in Chapter 3, applied to a far cheaper operation. Listing Listing shows both guarantees.

If the insert returns nothing, the request was a repeat, and a second query returns the original code. The counter value taken for the repeat is unused, and the code space allows those gaps. The other direction of the logic is the redirect, where the rules from Chapter 5 apply. A miss is loaded once under request coalescing, a confirmed absence is cached briefly, and a timeout is never mistaken for absence (Listing Listing).

The jitter on the lifetime spreads expiry so that entries written together do not all expire together, the same precaution as in Chapter 5.

How the Shortener Fails

A permanent redirect (HTTP status 301) permits caching that can bypass the service on later visits, which affects revocation and click measurements. For revocable links in this design, return a temporary redirect (302 or 307) with cache directives such as Cache-Control: no-store. The response status alone does not prevent caching. Test browser and intermediary behavior against the required disable delay.

Disabling a link raises a related problem. Deleting the row does nothing about copies already in the cache, so the link service has to define how long a disabled link may go on redirecting. If the policy permits stale redirects for the entire cache lifetime, an abusive link may continue redirecting until the cached entry expires. A shorter disable target requires active cache invalidation.

Bots add a third kind of trouble by probing random codes. Every unknown code is a cache miss that reaches the database, and the short negative entry in Listing Listing handles most of it. After a cache failure, the store receives the full peak request rate. At 9,600 lookups per second and a 5 ms lookup, about 48 are in flight on average, which exceeds the concurrency allocation of a pool sized for steady traffic. The recovery plan is the one from Chapter 5: bound the database’s concurrency, serve a small warm set first, and let the cache refill through request coalescing.

A queue transports click events for asynchronous aggregation. The reported click total may be approximate, since a redirect should complete without waiting for analytics. At-least-once delivery is acceptable when aggregation handles duplicate events and the product describes the reported totals accordingly. Abuse needs its own path as well. Destinations are scanned after creation rather than during it, and a finding feeds the same disable mechanism. Creation is also the cheapest place to stop abuse, so it is where per-account rate limits belong.

Assumption and scope & At least 90 percent of redirects are served from the cache, so the link store receives fewer than 1,

Condition that tests it & Cache loss, campaign traffic, or repeated scans change the miss rate.
Constraint or invariant & Bound store-read concurrency during ordinary misses and recovery after cache loss.
Evidence and uncertainty & Estimated from a 5×5\times5× peak factor and an assumed popularity skew. Not yet measured against production traffic.

Hit rate during campaigns, after cache loss, and under scanning. Whether the store’s read capacity covers a 50 percent hit rate.
Signal and evaluation window & Observe hit rate and store lookup rate over the stated ten-minute window.
Control and decision & If the hit rate is below 80 percent for ten minutes, add negative caching or read capacity before peak.
Owner and review trigger & The redirect-service owner, who also owns the disable-propagation time objective. Review after each failure drill and before increasing traffic.

A Social Timeline

What the Timeline Promises

When a customer opens the app, it shows recent posts from the accounts they follow, newest first, within the product’s response-time target. Every returned post must satisfy the customer’s access permissions. That last clause turns the problem from one of speed into one of correctness, and it will come back in a later subsection.

Sizing the Timeline

Suppose 20 million daily users. Each posts twice a day, opens the timeline ten times a day, and the authors of these posts have 200 followers on average, weighted by how often each author posts. An average across accounts alone would underestimate fan-out work if popular accounts post more frequently.

Reads outnumber posts five to one, which suggests a read-heavy system. The workload changes once the application materializes timelines at write time. If every new post is copied into each follower’s stored timeline at the moment it is written, a practice called fan-out on write, each post becomes about 200 inserts. Timeline inserts then occur at roughly forty times the rate of timeline reads. That is the trade in this design. We pay at write time, in bulk, so that each read becomes a single lookup.

The Fan-Out Bottleneck

The scarce resource is fan-out throughput, and the danger is what happens when a very large account posts. At 92,600 inserts per second, ten million follower inserts consume about 108 seconds of the fleet’s entire throughput, before accounting for ordinary posts. If that job monopolizes a first-in, first-out (FIFO) worker queue, ordinary posts wait behind it. Chunking and fair scheduling reduce that delay, but the ten million writes still have to be completed. Chapter 12 named this problem head-of-line blocking: one item at the front of an ordered line delays everything behind it.

Choosing Between Push, Pull, and Both

For ordinary accounts, a worker appends the post’s identifier to each follower’s stored timeline. Above a follower threshold, say several hundred thousand, the post skips fan-out and is recorded only in the author’s own list. When a customer opens the app, the feed service takes their precomputed timeline, pulls recent posts from the few large accounts they follow, merges the two by time, and loads the post bodies by identifier.

The threshold should come from measurement. Below it the read path is cheap and the write path pays, and above it the write path is protected and the read path pays, in proportion to how many large accounts the reader follows. A cap on how many large accounts one read will merge belongs in the design from the start, since without one the read path has no upper bound.

The Write and Read Paths

The timeline stores post identifiers, not posts, and the choice of structure makes a replay harmless. Adding a member to a sorted set with the creation time as its score is idempotent. A worker that crashes and replays its batch writes the same member with the same score, and nothing changes. We design toward that property wherever we can: choose a stored representation in which replaying a message changes nothing (Listing Listing).

The trim on every insert limits each timeline to 800 entries, which is where the 128 GB storage estimate came from. The final read step rechecks visibility because fan-out may have stored a post before the viewer lost permission to read it. The next subsection covers that case.

Visibility and Deletion

Permission changes affect timelines that were already written. Suppose a customer blocks someone, a post is deleted, or an account goes private. The stored timelines already contain identifiers the reader should no longer see. If permissions were checked only at fan-out time, we would be enforcing a decision made hours ago. So the read path checks visibility again, against the authoritative source, when it loads each post. The stored timeline is a hint about what might be shown, and the post store decides what may be shown.

Deletion works the same way. A deleted post leaves a tombstone, a marker saying the item is gone, and readers skip tombstoned identifiers. A background job removes the stale identifiers from timelines later, and nothing the customer sees waits for it.

How the Timeline Fails

The right measure of freshness is the delay between a post being accepted and its appearing in a follower’s timeline, at the 95th and 99th percentile. A queue depth of a million means little without the rate, so alerts should watch the age of the oldest unprocessed post, and separate queues or priorities should stop a large account from delaying ordinary ones.

A new user, or one whose stored timeline was evicted, has nothing to read. The timeline can be rebuilt from the authors they follow, under a concurrency limit, serving a reduced version first. Without the limit, a cache flush becomes a database outage, the same pattern as the cold-cache failures of Chapter 5.

Reading has its own amplification. A reader who follows 300 large accounts triggers 300 pulls on every timeline load. The cap on merged accounts bounds that cost, and the merge rule has to specify which accounts are included when the cap applies.

Follow and unfollow need a decision too. Following someone does not put their older posts into your stored timeline unless the design says it does. We decide which, write it down, and test that unfollowing removes their posts from the next read rather than merely the next fan-out.

Hidden assumptions

Assumption and scope & The fan-out fleet, sized for the average insert rate, meets a freshness objective because very large accounts bypass fan-out.
Condition that tests it & A high-follower account posts during peak demand, or a reader follows many large accounts.
Constraint or invariant & Bound work per fan-out batch and high-follower account pulls per read. Enforce visibility checks at read time.
Evidence and uncertainty & Derived from 463 posts per second and 200 average followers. The follower distribution is assumed, not measured.

The right follower threshold, the number of large accounts a typical reader follows, and behavior during an actual surge.
Signal and evaluation window & Observe post-to-visible delay, oldest fan-out job, and pulls per read over two consecutive configured evaluation windows.
Control and decision & Lower the threshold when post-to-visible delay exceeds the objective for two consecutive windows.
Owner and review trigger & The feed team owns freshness. The post-store owner owns visibility rules, and the read path must call them. Review after each failure drill and before increasing traffic.

A Notification Service

What Each Message Promises

The service delivers the right message to the right person through the channel they chose, once, in time for it to be useful. Every clause rules out a failure: wrong message, wrong person, wrong channel, duplicate, late. Different messages carry different consequences. For a one-time passcode, late is the same as lost. For a marketing message, a duplicate is an annoyance and a lost one goes unnoticed. The two kinds of message have different promises, which is a first hint that they should not share a queue.

Sizing the Service

Suppose 10 million notifications go out on an ordinary day, and a campaign adds 2 million more over ten minutes. The email provider accepts 1,000 messages per second for this account.

Estimates for the notification service. The completion-time estimate assumes the campaign has the whole provider allowance.

The Provider’s Limit

What runs out first is the provider’s rate limit, which everything the service sends must share. At campaign speed, demand is more than three times the allowance. If campaign mail and a login passcode share one queue and one allowance, a code-generation request can wait behind up to half an hour of marketing. The arithmetic makes the architectural argument before anyone draws a diagram.

Separating Message Classes

Each class of message gets its own queue and its own delivery deadline, and all classes draw on one allowance. The mechanism that stops campaigns from starving passcodes is a token bucket that reserves its last tokens for priority traffic. Transactional messages may take any token. Bulk messages may take a token only if enough are left to preserve the reserve (Listing Listing).

This version is not thread-safe, and a production one needs a lock or an atomic operation in a shared store, which also means deciding what happens to the allowance if that store fails over (Chapter 14). The priority reserve needs a workload test. With a rate of 1,000 per second, a bucket capacity of 1,000, reserve of 300, transactional traffic at 100 per second, and a campaign offering 3,333 per second, a simulation admitted every transactional message and about 900 campaign messages per second. The campaign takes about 37 minutes to complete, rather than 33, because the transactional traffic takes its share first. The reserve also acts as a burst cushion. When bulk traffic has reduced available tokens to the reserved floor, a burst of 400 transactional messages finds 300 tokens waiting and then continues at the refill rate.

Every message includes an operation identifier assigned when the request is accepted, a class, and an expiry. The worker checks the expiry before sending. A passcode that is valid for five minutes and has waited six is dropped and recorded as expired, not sent late (Listing Listing).

Duplicates, Losses, and Preferences

The hard case is the payment timeout from Chapter 3 again. A worker submits the message, but the provider call times out before the worker receives a result. If the provider supports an idempotency key with a sufficient retention period, the worker resubmits the same operation identifier under that contract. Otherwise, it must determine whether the original submission could still succeed. A negative status lookup is conclusive only when the provider documents the lookup scope and a completion bound for the earlier request, as Chapter 3 explains. When the provider cannot establish the outcome, the notification policy must choose between possible duplication and possible loss. For a login passcode, retrying may be preferable to blocking login, but duplicate messages can still confuse customers and trigger provider rate limits. A receipt should use the provider’s status lookup, if there is one, before resending. A marketing message can usually be allowed to go missing.

The two checks at the top are the preference rule. A customer who unsubscribes at 9:00 must not receive a campaign message that was accepted at 8:00 and dequeued at 9:05, so the worker checks the current preference and quiet hours at send time. The state names at the bottom are the precise vocabulary. “Accepted by the provider” is not “delivered,” and neither is “opened.” Record which of these each status means and report them separately. Delivery receipts often arrive late, so any report built from them should state its lag. Recording the attempt before calling the provider is what lets another worker pick up an UNKNOWN message after a crash.

How the Notification Service Fails

When the provider is down, queues lengthen, and the expiry rule bounds them. Expired passcodes are discarded instead of being sent after they can no longer be used. A second channel for transactional messages, such as text messages when email is down, is a reasonable fallback. It brings its own allowance and its own evidence of delivery, though, and it needs its own test before anyone relies on it.

A retry policy that resends on every timeout multiplies load on a provider that is already slow, so a single component owns retries, with a budget and a backoff (Chapter 4). Malformed templates and invalid addresses fail every time. After a bounded number of attempts they enter a quarantine with an owner (Chapter 12), and the queue continues processing.

Finally, every team in the company wants to send notifications. Without per-producer quotas, one faulty producer can consume the whole allowance. The quota belongs at acceptance, where rejecting a request is cheap.

Hidden assumptions

Assumption and scope & Reserving part of the provider allowance for transactional messages limits their delay to the delivery objective while a campaign runs.
Condition that tests it & A campaign burst overlaps transactional messages or the provider slows.
Constraint or invariant & All producers and message classes share the provider allowance. Apply expiry and preference checks before dispatch.
Evidence and uncertainty & Arithmetic and a simulation of one bucket: a 3,
333 per second campaign against a 1,000 per second limit. No test yet with the production provider. Still unknown: The provider’s enforcement window, retry treatment, and idempotency guarantees require verification.

Signal and evaluation window & Measure queue age by message class and provider acceptance through the ten-minute campaign burst and the subsequent recovery period.
Control and decision & Page when the age of the oldest transactional message exceeds the objective.
Owner and review trigger & The notification-platform team owns allocation. Each producing team owns its quota and its content. Review after each failure drill and before increasing traffic.

A Centralized Change-Validation Platform

An engineering organization has three different descriptions of its deployment rules. Jenkins checks a configuration file in the pipeline repository. A Slack bot reads a separately maintained list of restricted changes. Jira records the approvals associated with production releases. A deployment passes the Jenkins check while the Slack bot reports that the same change is prohibited. An engineer investigates and discovers that the tools have different revisions of the policy. The organization wants a central validation service that prevents unauthorized deployments and provides an audit trail for each decision.

This problem is deliberately outside the Baodium checkout path. It uses the same foundational ideas, but its central operation is a permission decision whose validity can change between evaluation and execution. Consider an initial proposal before reading the implementation. It needs a way to represent policy, an API for evaluating a change, an authoritative source of approvals, a durable record of decisions, and a place where deployment is stopped when validation fails. Which of those elements must be part of one transaction, and which can be updated later?

The Product Contract and Its Authority

The organization establishes four guarantees. First, an administrator can publish an immutable policy revision, and the service identifies one active revision for each target environment. Second, a change is evaluated against an identified policy revision and a stable digest of its inputs. Third, Jenkins must request authorization just before the protected deployment operation, and a decision made under an obsolete revision cannot silently authorize execution. Fourth, every decision retains enough evidence to reconstruct the policy and inputs used, within the organization’s retention and privacy requirements.

The service has three decision outcomes. ALLOW means the evaluated inputs satisfy the applicable policy and required approval evidence. DENY means authoritative evidence establishes a policy violation. INDETERMINATE means the service cannot establish a permitted or prohibited result because required evidence is unavailable or incomplete. Jenkins must refuse protected execution for both DENY and INDETERMINATE. It can present different explanations and retry procedures, but neither outcome grants permission.

Slack is an informational interface and Jira is a source of approval evidence under the organization’s documented integration contract. Neither is the policy publisher. An authentication layer identifies the caller, an administrative role publishes policy, and a deployment role requests execution authorization. Server-side authorization checks the caller’s permission for the requested environment and artifact. A request that names a valid change ID does not acquire permission merely by knowing that ID.

Deriving the Records

A policy revision contains an immutable body, digest, author, publication time, and precedence rules. An active pointer identifies the revision currently applicable to an environment. A change identifies an artifact digest, target service, environment, actor, and the approval references it claims. An evaluation records the policy revision, input digest, decision, reasons, and evidence version or retrieval time. An authorization identifies the exact deployment target and the conditions under which execution may proceed. Finally, a connector observation records which published revision an integration has observed.

These are distinct records because the events they represent occur at different times. One change can be evaluated again after a policy revision. One evaluation can be rendered in Slack without granting deployment permission. One authorization can expire or become invalid while the historical evaluation is still valid as an account of what the earlier policy decided.

A relational schema can enforce much of this contract with primary keys, foreign keys, uniqueness constraints, and transactions. A minimal PostgreSQL representation of the authoritative records appears below. Approval payloads and more detailed policy evaluation results can be stored in additional tables. Those omissions do not change the need for immutable identities and recorded revisions.

CREATE TABLE policy_revision (
    revision bigint PRIMARY KEY,
    environment text NOT NULL,
    body_sha256 text NOT NULL,
    body_json jsonb NOT NULL,
    published_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    UNIQUE(environment, revision)
);
CREATE TABLE active_policy (
    environment text PRIMARY KEY,
    revision bigint NOT NULL,
    FOREIGN KEY (environment, revision)
        REFERENCES policy_revision(environment, revision)
);
CREATE TABLE change_request (
    change_id uuid PRIMARY KEY,
    environment text NOT NULL,
    artifact_sha256 text NOT NULL,
    target_service text NOT NULL,
    created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE TABLE evaluation (
    evaluation_id uuid PRIMARY KEY,
    change_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES change_request(change_id),
    request_key text NOT NULL,
    input_sha256 text NOT NULL,
    policy_revision bigint NOT NULL
        REFERENCES policy_revision(revision),
    decision text NOT NULL CHECK
        (decision IN ('ALLOW', 'DENY', 'INDETERMINATE')),
    evaluated_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    UNIQUE(change_id, request_key)
);
CREATE TABLE deployment_authorization (
    authorization_id uuid PRIMARY KEY,
    evaluation_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES evaluation(evaluation_id),
    target_sha256 text NOT NULL,
    expires_at timestamptz NOT NULL,
    consumed_at timestamptz
);
CREATE TABLE connector_observation (
    environment text NOT NULL,
    connector_id text NOT NULL,
    observed_revision bigint NOT NULL,
    observed_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    PRIMARY KEY(environment, connector_id)
);

The schema alone cannot make a deployment safe. The application has to verify that an authorization’s evaluation belongs to the same environment and target, that the caller may use it, and that the active revision and expiry satisfy the current execution policy. Changes to the active revision need transactional serialization with any operation whose contract requires publication and execution to be mutually ordered. If physical deployment execution occurs later in another system, a database transaction cannot cover the entire external action. A bounded authorization with revalidation at the execution boundary narrows that interval, and the residual race must be handled under a documented policy. For stronger guarantees, the protected deployment controller must participate in an enforcement protocol that can prevent execution after revocation.

An API That Distinguishes Evaluation from Execution

The initial API can use four operations. POST /policies publishes a revision under administrative authorization. POST /evaluations records an immutable assessment. GET /evaluations/{id} retrieves that assessment. POST /deployments/authorize checks whether a previous evaluation is permitted to authorize a particular target now. Additional endpoints can report active revisions and connector observations. The last endpoint is the enforcement boundary, and Jenkins cannot replace it with a cached result from an earlier validation step.

The shortened digests are illustrative placeholders, not full SHA-256 values that an implementation should accept. A production API would use full digests and would define how request canonicalization produces the input hash. Repeating the same request key with an identical payload returns the recorded evaluation. Using that key with a different input digest returns a conflict rather than silently reusing permission for another artifact.

Choosing the First Architecture

The initial deployment can be a modular application with an API served over HTTP Secure (HTTPS), a PostgreSQL authority store, a durable outbox, and a reconciliation worker. Authentication and role checks run before publication or authorization. Policy evaluation uses immutable rule revisions and documented precedence. An administrator’s emergency restriction may outrank a tenant-level allowance, for example, but precedence must be modeled in the policy language and tested against conflicting rules. Sorting rules by creation time would make outcomes depend on incidental insertion order and could silently grant unsafe access.

Large policy bundles or evidence artifacts may justify object storage such as S3, indexed by revision and verified by digest. Frequently retrieved immutable revisions may be served from process memory or Redis. The cache must never replace the authoritative active-revision check for protected execution. SQS can carry independent integration tasks when bounded retries and delivery are sufficient. Kafka becomes a candidate when independent consumers require retained replay and ordered histories within a chosen partition key. None of these additions changes who may publish a policy or authorize deployment.

The request rate for policy publication may be small, while evaluation demand can be bursty during release windows. Consider 200 teams producing an average of ten change evaluations a day. That is only about 2,000 evaluations per day, or 0.023 per second averaged across a day. Yet if 1,000 validations arrive within five minutes of a release window, the offered rate during that period is about 3.33 per second. Database selection is unlikely to be driven by raw request throughput at this scale. Reproducible decisions, constraints, transactional authority, and operational simplicity matter more. The workload estimate must be revisited if policy evaluation becomes a low-latency check inside every deployment step for a much larger engineering organization.

The Revision-17 Failure Drill

The initial proposal performs evaluations correctly during ordinary traffic. Now an administrator publishes revision 18, which prohibits the deployment that revision 17 permitted. Jenkins still has an earlier ALLOW response. If Jenkins treats that response as permanent permission, the central service has recorded the new rule but cannot enforce it. This is a time-of-check/time-of-use problem: the condition evaluated earlier may no longer be true when the protected action starts.

An improved protocol binds the authorization to the change ID, artifact digest, target environment, policy revision, and a short validity interval. The execution gateway checks those conditions and the active revision just before permitting the protected action. Revisions that prohibit previously approved changes may invalidate outstanding authorization records. If the policy requires revocation to prevent an action after it has passed the final check, the deployment controller needs an additional enforcement point during execution. A signed token alone cannot establish revocation if the controller accepts it offline until expiry.

There is a choice to make about active changes. Some organizations may permit a previously authorized deployment to finish after publication of new rules. Others require new restrictions to take effect before any further action. The published policy contract must define which behavior applies. The system cannot make this choice from an HTTP status code or a cache TTL.

Reconciliation and Production Review

The platform should periodically compare the desired revision for each integration with the version that connector reports. A difference is an audit finding, not automatic evidence of an unauthorized deployment. The worker records its scan interval, integration identity, observed revision, and repair attempt. It repeats incomplete scans without creating duplicate active cases for the same discrepancy. Jenkins must still ask the authority whether a specific deployment can execute, even after its local policy projection is repaired.

The service’s principal measurements include the proportion of protected executions with a verified authorization, evaluation latency by outcome, indeterminate decisions by dependency, age of integration drift, and time to reconcile incomplete operations. An authorization failure that prevents execution should be visible to the release owner and support a documented remediation procedure. Persistent dependence on Jira during every enforcement request may cause avoidable unavailability, so an organization may maintain signed, time-bounded approval evidence within the validation authority when its security contract permits it. The freshness and revocation limits of that evidence must then be tested.

The resulting architecture is relatively small. It has one authoritative policy source, one place that grants protected execution, durable evaluation history, and repairable integrations. More services or brokers can be introduced when their requirements are established. A reader who chose different components can still defend the design by explaining the authority model, consistency constraints, failure responses, workload, and operational evidence. That is the same review applied to the shortener, timeline, notification service, and Baodium’s European launch.

What the Designs Have in Common

Putting the designs side by side, the same engineering decisions appear in different forms.

The arithmetic named the constraint before we chose any component. For the shortener it was the cache hit rate, for the timeline it was fan-out throughput, and for the notification service it was a provider allowance we do not control. None of them was the database, which is where most whiteboard discussions begin.

Each design also protected one class of work from another. Campaigns cannot starve passcodes, celebrity posts cannot starve ordinary ones, and analytics cannot slow redirects. Every one of those protections is a reservation or a separate path, and each costs some utilization that we accepted on purpose.

Operations used the same identities across retries, and wherever we could arrange it the stored representation made a replay harmless. The dependency whose outcome can be unknown was named, and the class of message or request decided the policy for it. The review recorded each decision with its requirements and supporting evidence. A new workload or failure condition may justify a different choice.

And the measure of success was never a component metric. It was disable-propagation time, post-to-visible delay, and the age of the oldest passcode, each stated in seconds and each something a customer would notice.

You can use the same five questions on a design you have never seen. We start with the promise, compute the numbers, find the resource that runs out, and ask what an operation’s identity is. The boxes and arrows can wait until the end.
